| [LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md) | Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2001), Cambridge University Press. The book-length statement of picoeconomics: hyperbolic discounting makes a person a population of bargaining interests, and will is the recursive bundling of choices into precedents. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and the précis, [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md), which stands in for it. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from the publisher's description and from the outline of the book given in its précis, not read. Not open access: Unpaywall reports no open copy, and no author deposit of the book was found (the author's site, picoeconomics.org, carries the précis and articles, not the book). The owner suggested the précis instead, and it is read and filed as [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), which follows the book's three sections and twelve chapters. The book is kept as the citation others reach for. A human with library access could read chapters 5-8 (the bargaining model and its evidence) against the précis. |
| [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), the précis of Breakdown of Will (2001). People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Willpower is the bundling of future choices by treating the present one as a precedent: an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma, not an organ or a top-down ego. The same recursion predicts the will's costs: legalism, circumscribed "lapse districts", motivated blindness to lapses, and rules that favour countable goals over subtle ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), as the substitute for the 2001 book ([LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md)), which the owner suggested and which the précis follows chapter by chapter. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". The same mechanism predicts the will's side effects: legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control. |
| [LIT-589](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-589.md) | Goal Striving, Need Satisfaction, and Longitudinal Well-Being: The Self-Concordance Model | Sheldon & Elliot (1999), JPSP 76(3):482–497. A goal is self-concordant when pursued for identified or intrinsic rather than external or introjected reasons. In three semester-long studies of students, self-concordance predicted sustained effort, which fully mediated its link to attainment; attainment raised well-being more when goals were self-concordant; and accumulated daily experiences of autonomy, competence and relatedness partly mediated attainment's effect on well-being. Paths survived controls for self-efficacy, implementation intentions, avoidance framing and life skills. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-448](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-448.md)); worth reading as the canonical statement of the self-concordance model and its evidence. Goals pursued for identified or intrinsic reasons get more sustained effort, so are better attained (effort fully mediates, in Studies 1 and 3), and attaining them raises well-being more, partly through accumulated daily experiences of autonomy, competence and relatedness. The evidence is three semester-long correlational studies of students (N = 169, 152, 73), with structural models refitted after modification indices, and self-concordance is a self-report of reasons that cannot separate integration from identification. |
| [LIT-592](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-592.md) | The Authentic Personality: A Theoretical and Empirical Conceptualization and the Development of the Authenticity Scale | Wood, Linley, Maltby, Baliousis & Joseph (2008), Journal of Counseling Psychology 55(3):385–399. Unread. Every lawful copy found is out of reach: Manchester's portal lists a pre-peer-review manuscript (PRE-PEER-REVIEW.PDF, 143 KB) whose download is behind a JavaScript and cookie challenge, which I did not try to get past; Stirling's STORRE holds the published version under a permanent embargo ("The publisher does not allow this work to be made publicly available"); Warwick's WRAP and Lincoln's repository records carry no file; ResearchGate refused the request. | [LIT-595](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-595.md) | “First we invented stories, then they changed us”: The Evolution of Narrative Identity | McAdams (2019), Evolutionary Studies in Imaginative Culture 3(1):1–18. Narrative identity is "the internalized and evolving story a person invents to explain how he or she has become the person he or she is becoming", giving a life "unity, moral purpose, and temporal coherence". Storytelling evolved with human hypersociality. The self develops from social actor (by age 2) to motivated agent (school years) to autobiographical author (adolescence). Agentic and redemptive stories go with well-being and generativity, and cultures supply master narratives. "Biology guides and culture fills in the details." | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-470](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-470.md)), as the read substitute for McAdams & McLean, "Narrative Identity" (2013; [LIT-572](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-572.md)), which has no lawful copy and whose definition this essay takes over word for word. Worth reading as McAdams's own short statement of narrative identity: "the internalized and evolving story a person invents to explain how he or she has become the person he or she is becoming", which gives a life "unity, moral purpose, and temporal coherence". It places the life story as the third layer of a self that develops from actor to agent to author, and reports that story features (agency, redemption, coherence) predict well-being and generativity. A review essay: the empirical claims are cited, not shown, and the evolutionary story is offered as plausible, not tested. |
| [LIT-602](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-602.md) | The Intimate Contest for Self-Command | Schelling (1980), The Public Interest, Summer 1980, pp. 94-118. People behave sometimes "as if they had two selves" in "continual contest for control", and the tactics of self-management (removing the option, bright lines, monitoring, delays, raising the stakes) are the tactics of managing someone else. A single-dimension model of impatience fits poorly. Which self is authentic is left open. Failures of consumer self-management may be worth "on the order of a trillion dollars". | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-452](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-452.md)), in place of the 1984 Ely Lecture ([LIT-573](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-573.md)), which has no lawful free copy. Worth reading as Schelling's own first statement of "egonomics": a person sometimes behaves "as if they had two selves" that alternate in command, and the tactics people use on themselves (mittens, alarm clocks across the room, bright lines, Christmas savings, deadlines, delays) are the tactics they use to manage another person. It refuses to say which self is authentic in general, and it gives an order-of-magnitude estimate that failures of consumer self-management cost as much as all other consumer-ignorance problems together. |
| [LIT-604](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-604.md) | Control theory: A useful conceptual framework for personality–social, clinical, and health psychology | Carver & Scheier (1982), Psychological Bulletin 92(1):111-135. A review arguing, by its title, that control theory is a useful framework for personality-social, clinical and health psychology. | [LIT-606](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-606.md) | Thine Own Self: True Self-Concept Accessibility and Meaning in Life | Schlegel, Hicks, Arndt & King (2009), JPSP 96(2):473–490. Five studies: faster "me" judgments for one's own true-self traits (residualized on speed for control traits) predict presence of meaning in life, while actual-self accessibility does not, controlling affect, need satisfaction and (Study 4) AI-3 authenticity, which was itself uncorrelated with true-self accessibility. Subliminal priming of true-self traits raised reported meaning (Studies 3 and 5), for disliked traits as much as liked ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-469](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-469.md)); worth reading as the experimental case that the true self-concept, as distinct from self-reported authenticity, matters to felt meaning. In five student studies (N = 56 to 149), how quickly people classify their own "true self" traits predicts presence of meaning in life over and above actual-self accessibility, need satisfaction and AI-3 authenticity, and subliminally priming true-self traits raises reported meaning, even when the traits are disliked. | [LIT-696](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-696.md) | Towards a Theory of Collective Emotions | von Scheve & Ismer (2013), Emotion Review 5(4):406–413. Collective emotion is synchronous convergence in affective responding towards an event or object. Three literatures (face-to-face contagion and effervescence, culture and shared knowledge, social identification) are recast as bottom-up mechanisms on three levels: social cognition (shared appraisals; collectively intentional appraisals), expressive behaviour (contagion, "facial dialects") and symbolic practice (collective memory, group-based sentiments, norms, cultural sharing). Mutual awareness and group membership amplify convergence and can turn I-mode into We-mode collective emotion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-552](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-552.md)); worth reading as a compact map of how collective emotion has been theorised across sociology, social psychology and philosophy, and as the source of a working definition: collective emotion is synchronous convergence in affective responding across individuals towards one event or object. Shared appraisal structures give the minimal case. Mutual awareness (contagion, sharing) and group membership (identity, collective intention, norms, collective memory, sentiments) amplify it and can turn "I-mode" into "We-mode" collective emotion. A conceptual synthesis with no data, built bottom-up by methodological choice. |

Introduces emotional aperture, the ability to recognise the composition of diverse emotions in a collective such as a group or business unit, and argues that a leader's ability to respond to the patterns of shared emotion that arise in strategic change depends on it. Describes cultural, psychological and contextual enablers and impediments, and extends emotional competencies beyond the individual level. Unread: from the abstract. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-04 from bibliographic records and the publisher's abstract, not read. No lawful full text was reachable. The 2006 working-paper version (Ross School of Business Paper No. 1047, "Emotional Aperture and Strategic Renewal", SSRN 931492) is on SSRN, which returned 403 to this session, and a Deep Blue item the search found, "Emotional Aperture and Emotional Sequencing" (handle 2027.42/48737), sits behind a bot challenge, which I did not try to pass. ProQuest's open preview carries the citation only. A human with library access, or anyone opening the SSRN working paper in a browser, could read it, and that reading would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-700.md) | Three kinds of collective attitudes | List (2014), Erkenntnis 79(S9):1601–1622. Collective attitudes come in three kinds. Aggregate attitudes summarise members' attitudes by a rule or a market, supervene proposition-wise and need not be rational. Common attitudes are held by all members with common awareness, matter for coordination, and inherit consistency from their unanimity. Corporate attitudes belong to a group agent, guide its action, supervene holistically on members' contributions and must be rational. The kinds are almost logically independent, and fears and hopes divide the same way as beliefs and desires. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-554.md)); worth reading as the disambiguation the collective-attitudes literature needs: aggregate attitudes (summaries, supervening proposition by proposition), common attitudes (unanimous and commonly known, supervening on a slightly enriched base) and corporate attitudes (a group agent's, supervening holistically and not straightforwardly reducible). The three are almost logically independent. A review by its own description, with no new theorem; its value for this record is that it names fears and hopes among the attitudes the split applies to, which gives the collective-emotion debate a vocabulary. |
| [LIT-703](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-703.md) | Emotion in the Workplace: A Reappraisal | Ashforth & Humphrey (1995), Human Relations 48(2):97–125. Organisations treat emotion as the antithesis of rationality, and so regulate it through four institutionalised mechanisms: neutralizing, buffering, prescribing and normalizing emotion. Against this, emotionality and rationality are "interpenetrated", emotion is an inseparable part of organisational life and often functional for the organisation, as shown for motivation, leadership and group dynamics. Unread: from the abstract. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-04 from bibliographic records and the publisher's abstract, not read. No lawful full text was reachable. Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar list no open copy. A web search found only ResearchGate (not used) and a 2014 Arizona State syllabus that lists the paper but does not carry it. SAGE does not make the article open. A human with library access could read it (29 pages) and move this to Active. |
| [LIT-705](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-705.md) | Group Agency and Supervenience | List & Pettit (2006), Southern Journal of Philosophy 44(S1):85–105. A group agent's rationality must supervene on its members' contributions, but not proposition by proposition. Three impossibility results show that robust group rationality (complete, consistent, deductively closed group judgments for every profile of rational member judgments) is inconsistent with majoritarian, uniform proposition-wise and proposition-wise supervenience. Premise-based and distributed premise-based procedures show it is consistent with set-wise supervenience, with group judgments that can be discontinuous with the members' judgments on the same proposition. Emergent agency without any member's conception of the group is set aside as unintelligible. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-550.md)); worth reading as the short, formal core of List and Pettit's group agency: a group can be a robustly rational judge only if its judgment on a proposition is not, in general, a function of its members' judgments on that proposition. Group judgments supervene on members' judgments set-wise, not proposition-wise, so a group agent is individualistically unmysterious and still "not directly continuous" with its members. Read here as the lawful substitute for the unread book [LIT-391](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-391.md), whose chapter 3 takes up the same supervenience question; the impossibility results are cited from other papers, not proved here. |
| [LIT-706](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-706.md) | The Ripple Effect: Emotional Contagion and its Influence on Group Behavior | Barsade (2002), Administrative Science Quarterly 47(4):644–675. Two studies of mood contagion in a leaderless group negotiation. In Study 1 (94 undergraduates, 29 groups) a trained confederate showed pleasant or unpleasant, high- or low-energy mood. Members' mood moved with the confederate's valence, by self-report and by blind video-coders, and pleasant contagion predicted more cooperation, less conflict and higher self-rated performance. Study 2 (113 MBA students, 26 groups, no confederate) found mood convergence (ICC .00 to .24) with the same process correlates. Members recognised that others influenced how pleasant they felt, but not that their mood shaped their judged effectiveness. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-551](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-551.md)), from the August 2001 revise-and-resubmit manuscript Wharton deposited in Penn's repository, not the published version; worth reading as the first causal test of emotional contagion in groups. A trained confederate's pleasant or unpleasant mood spread to the members of 29 work groups (self-report and blind video-coders agree), and the more pleasant mood spread, the more cooperative and the less conflicted the group (coder-rated) and the better members rated their own performance. A second study without a confederate found members' moods converging (ICC .00 before, .24 after). Members related their pleasantness to others' conduct but showed no awareness of their mood's bearing on how effective they judged themselves (manuscript p. 37). Valence and energy hypotheses failed or came out mixed. |
